newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai markets take a breather, but worse to come.
newsitem.headline: Thai markets take a breather, but worse to come.

text.p: Pundits may have been surprised when Thailand's beleaguered stock market turned higher on Friday. But many just shrug their shoulders and predict more pain as mounting debt problems tear through the economy.
"It beats me!" said Graham Catterwell, country manager for Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, when asked why buyers had returned to the bourse on a day when it had been expected to plummet.
"There's worse to come. Property prices have to come down. Many companies are teetering on the verge of bankruptcy. The SET index has come down and it could go down further," he said.
The SET share index shrugged off a plunge in shares of debt-crippled Finance One Plc on Friday to end almost 1.5 percent higher at 566.39, its best gain in seven nervous sessions.

Analysts said the market could consolidate around current levels, its lowest for nearly eight years, before taking another cold shower under news of continued economic slowdown, shrinking corporate earnings and corporate debt problems.

The collapse of plans to rescue the once-glorious Finance One by merging it with a commercial bank has renewed concern about the risk of insolvency and liquidity runs at many of the country's cash-strapped finance companies.

Thailand's 15 local banks and 91 finance firms have extended a massive 800 billion baht ($31 billion) in loans to the crisis-torn property market, and analysts reckon that 20 percent of finance companies' loans are non-performing.

Without the spate of mergers that the authorities had been counting on to nurse the sector back to health, the central Bank of Thailand may have to dig deep into its coffers to guarantee deposits and ensure stability.

Sriyan Pietersz of Capital Nomura Securities argued in a recent report that the central bank's ability to come good on its guarantee would be stretched in a prolonged liquidity run, given that deposits total more than $40 billion.

"Under such circumstances, a wave of small and medium-sized financial company failures -- with a knock-on impact to their commercial bank and corporate shareholders -- does not seem unlikely," he wrote.
According to newspaper reports at the end of last week, the central bank may be about to bite the bullet, allowing as many as 30 financial firms to go under instead of bailing them out.
"Under the plan, only the deposits of the weakest firms would be guaranteed as the funds required to keep them all afloat would break the central bank," the Bangkok Post said.
The central bank has declined to confirm the reports.
The troubles of finance firms and the property sector aside, analysts say a host of other problems, linked to the economy's high-gearing and high interest rates, are coming home to roost.
A growing number of companies are missing debt payments and analysts point to a reported jump in the number of bounced cheques as evidence of growing cashflow difficulties.
Mounting debt could feed the economic slowdown by cutting into investment, jobs and domestic demand.
The government recently pared its forecast for economic growth this year to 5.9 percent from 6.4 percent in 1995. But private economists say it could be much lower, perhaps as low as three percent.
"Under the current economic reality...it is likely that the extent of the problems becoming more apparent today will escalate in coming months," said Momura's Pietersz.

"...the path to recovery will be studded with numerous corporate insolvencies and a deepening contraction in profitability growth," he said. "Under the circumstances, investors are unlikely to be hasty in returning to the SET -- or indeed in remaining invested."
